title: Search Every Entry
content:
What problem does this solve?
Printing every evidence index by hand works for two clues and falls apart for twenty. A for loop runs the same block once for each value in a list.

Basic syntax
  for clue in evidence:
      print(clue)

What actually happens
Python takes the first value in evidence, binds it to clue, and runs the indented block. Then it repeats with the next value, until the list is finished. The loop variable holds the current item, not an index.

When this is useful
Use a for loop whenever you want to do the same thing to every item — print them, format a line for each one, or make a small decision about the current clue. You already know if/else; combining it inside a loop is ordinary program composition, not a brand-new topic.
concepts: for item in a_list repeats a block once per value
The loop variable holds the current item, not an index
The indented block is the work that repeats

examples.title: Evidence collection
examples.code:
evidence = [
    "broken lantern",
    "drag marks",
    "gray dust",
    "torn cloak",
]
for clue in evidence:
    print(clue)
examples.explanation: The block runs four times — once for each clue, in order.

common_mistakes: Forgetting the colon after the for line
Forgetting to indent the repeated line
Printing the whole list once instead of looping over items

exercises.title: Predict the scan
exercises.prompt: What does this print? Type each line of output.
exercises.expected_answer:
broken lantern
drag marks
gray dust
hints: The loop body runs once per item, in order.
Each print ends a line, so you get one clue per line.
Three iterations: broken lantern, then drag marks, then gray dust.

exercises.title: Repair the loop
exercises.prompt: This program is supposed to print each clue on its own line, but it prints the whole list once. Fix it so the loop prints the current item.
hints: Look at what is being printed inside the loop.
The loop variable already holds the current clue.
Print clue each time, not evidence.

tests.message: Keep a for loop that visits each clue.

tests.expected:
broken lantern
drag marks
gray dust

exercises.title: Create an evidence report
exercises.prompt:
evidence is already created. Print these three lines using a for loop and an f-string:
Evidence: broken lantern
Evidence: drag marks
Evidence: gray dust
exercises.starter_code:
evidence = ["broken lantern", "drag marks", "gray dust"]
# Print a labeled line for each clue
hints: Loop over evidence so clue is each string in turn.
An f-string can start with Evidence: and insert the current clue.
Print once inside the loop, not three separate print calls.

tests.message: Use a for loop so the work repeats for each clue.
Build each line with an f-string.

tests.expected:
Evidence: broken lantern
Evidence: drag marks
Evidence: gray dust

exercises.title: Flag a suspicious entry
exercises.prompt:
evidence is already created. Loop through every clue. When the clue is "gray dust", print:
FLAG: gray dust

For every other clue, print:
logged: <clue>

Use a for loop and if/else. Build each line with an f-string.
exercises.starter_code:
evidence = ["broken lantern", "drag marks", "gray dust", "torn cloak"]
# Scan each clue; flag gray dust
hints: Inside the loop, ask whether the current clue equals "gray dust".
Use if/else so exactly one labeled line prints per clue.
Print f"FLAG: {clue}" for gray dust and f"logged: {clue}" otherwise.

tests.message: Use a for loop to visit each clue.
Use if/else inside the loop to choose FLAG or logged.
Build each output line with an f-string.

tests.expected:
logged: broken lantern
logged: drag marks
FLAG: gray dust
logged: torn cloak

exercises.success_message: Scan complete. Ordinary clues are logged; gray dust is flagged.
